newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Opposition coalition blasts Milosevic at rally.
newsitem.headline: Opposition coalition blasts Milosevic at rally.

text.p: Opposition leaders slammed Serbian President Slobodan Milosevic at a final election rally in Belgrade on Thursday, accusing him turning the country into a penniless police state.

Three days before rump Yugoslavia's federal and local elections, thousands of people gathered in Republic Square in the city centre to hear speakers for the opposition coalition rail against Milosevic's nine-year rule.

"God is wondering, what happened to these people in Serbia who let themselves be ruled by one man who can hold us in fear?" said Zoran Djindjic, of the Democratic Party. "We have to say to the world that it is past. This is it."
Leaders of the "Together" coalition predicted the four main opposition parties would emerge victorious in Sunday's vote but the crowd's subdued mood showed their previous disappointments.
For the first time, an opposition running the political spectrum from liberal to right-wing nationalist has managed to unite its forces against Milosevic.
The coalition, which also has the support of independent trade unions, has drawn large crowds at dozens of campaign rallies across the remainign Yugoslav republics of Serbia and Montenegro.
But the opposition cannot reach most voters because it was shut out from state television and radio, which ignored Thursday's rally.
Vuk Draskovic, who leads the largest opposition party, the Serbian Renewal Movement, accused Milosevic and his Marxist wife of creating a land of evil mired in the communist past.
He described Milosevic's leftist coalition as a group of "miserable people" trying to sow hatred and resurrect World War Two-era divisions between anti-Nazi partisans and royalist "chetniks".
"They are calling for hatred, new trenches and new divisions," Draskovic said. "They want to step back to 1941. They don't want to step forward to the 21st century."
After the disastrous wars that accompanied the collapse of the Yugoslav federation and sparked deep divisions among Serbs, Draskovic said it was time for reconciliation.
The opposition leaders ridiculed television advertising that celebrated Milosevic as a peacemaker while ignoring his role in the wars in Bosnia and Croatia.
"It's easy to be a peacemaker when you lost a war and made your people homeless," said Vesna Pesic, head of the Civic Alliance.
The opposition campaign has focused primarily on the poor state of the country's economy which has forced a third of the population into penury.
Many in the crowd recalled protests in the same square in 1991 that Milosevic crushed with tanks.
One elderly woman said she doubted if the opposition would win. But she said Milosevic's hold on power was eroding because of plummeting living standards.

"I'm not really sure we'll win this time," said 74-year old Radmila, who described herself as a longtime supporter of the opposition. "But maybe this will be the beginning. Things can't stay the way they are now."
